subject: JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?

messages.author: 9febcbf26d2ccc5b
messages.subject: JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
parts:
I have a Bayesian network DAG structure, and a conditional probability distribution (CPD) for each node.  I want to fit the parameters of the CPDs with a Bayesian method, since I have some prior knowledge on the parameters.  I implemented my procedure in Stan.  But I wonder, would it not be preferable to fit the procedure in JAGS?

My thinking is that the joint distribution in a Bayesian network can be decomposed into the product of conditional probabilities of each node given its parents in the graph.  The parameters of the CPDs for all the child-parents are independent (usual assumption in graphical models).  So you can have a separate posterior for the parameters of each CPD, conditional on the child and parent nodes.  

I'm thinking the Hamiltonian MCMC wouldn't make use of this parameter independence while a Gibbs sampler could.  This might make JAGs preferable to Stan when fitting a BN with more nodes.  Anyone have any insight?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
parts:
Let’s say you’re even luckier and you can exactly sample from each
of those conditional distributions.  How well will a Gibbs sampler do?

Well, conditioned on the values of the parents you can very quickly
generate new values for the child.  But then you have to generate
new values for the parents based on the children’s values.  Not only
is p(parent | child) not something you have in closed form, any
numerical approximation will require communicating with all of the
children.  So this will probably be slow.

Then you repeat, but because the parents are moving only very
slowly you explore the _joint_ distribution only very slowly.  It can
still take a very long time to generate a nearly independent sample
from the parents, which is the same time it takes for the conditional
distributions of the children to convolve together to generate a nearly
independent sample from their _marginal_ distributions.

In other words, conditional samples aren’t that informative when you
want to sample the entire model.  Especially when you have lots of
parameters.  This is a fundamental weakness of Gibbs sampling
that in some real respects can never be avoided (there are sort of
exceptions, but they tend to be subtle and can be argued to be
different problems entirely).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
parts:
That intuition is common, but backwards. It is crucial
in higher dimensions to move all the parameters in
a coordinated way, which Gibbs can't do with conditional
sampling.

Just imagine a simple hierarchical regression. The
hierarchical mean needs to move up and down with the lower
level coefficients (non-centered parameterizations help mitigate
this problem in both Gibbs and HMC). If you move the lower
level coefficients around the hierarchical mean, then the
hierarchical mean won't move much. The higher the dimensionality,
the more diffusive the whole thing is.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
parts: I don't follow what you mean by "parent".  Let's assume X is a node in a DAG with only one observed parent Y.  With the CPD, P(Y|X, μ) where μ is a parameter.  You are saying that I'd sample from P(μ, Y | X) right?  But why would I do that?  Both Y and X are observed in data.  So I'd sample from P(μ | X, Y) right?  Even if that weren't in closed form, it seems to have the advantage of implicitly encoding in the MCMC that μ depends on X and Y and only and not other variable in the data.

In general, you only need the Markov blanket to evaluate
a conditional density up to a constant. And you only
draw a sample of the parameters, not the data.

You have exactly N total parameters, each of which is independent of
the others conditioned only on data? That's just fitting N
completely independent univariate models. In which case by all means fit
them separately.

- Bob
